# Flight turbulence report (pre-flight or in-flight)

## Inputs
- Flight number, airline, and date (from the calendar, a booking confirmation, or the user).
- Whether the flight is domestic (US only) or international, and whether it is already airborne.

## Steps
1. **Find qualifying flights.** When run from a schedule, check the calendar for the target flight. If a report for that exact flight and date was already sent in this chat, stop silently.
2. **Get the route and position.** Try FlightAware first, though its page may show only origin and destination. Then try FlightRadar24 or ADS-B Exchange (a browser may be needed) for the filed route, waypoint coordinates, cruise altitude, live position, and times. For oceanic flights, free ADS-B feeds (adsb.lol, adsb.fi) usually show nothing and airplanes.live needs access. FlightRadar24 worked (live position, flown track, ETA): look up by callsign, e.g. https://data-cloud.flightradar24.com/zones/fcgi/feed.js?callsign=ICE656 , then https://data-live.flightradar24.com/clickhandler/?flight=<id> for the track. Airline callsigns use the ICAO prefix plus the number (e.g. ICE for Icelandair, DAL for Delta). If no route is found, assume the airline's typical routing and say so.
3. **Pull advisories along the route.**
   - **Domestic US:** aviationweather.gov SIGMETs, convective SIGMETs, AIRMETs (Tango) and G-AIRMETs, PIREPs, and wind and temperature charts.
   - **International or oceanic** (US AIRMETs do not apply):
     - Worldwide international SIGMETs: https://aviationweather.gov/api/data/isigmet?format=raw&hazard=turb . Filter by the airspace codes the route crosses, e.g. BIRD (Iceland), CZQX (Gander Oceanic), CZUL (Montreal), BGGL (Greenland), EGGX (Shanwick), CZEG/CZWG (Edmonton/Winnipeg).
     - Airport conditions and forecasts for any ICAO code: https://aviationweather.gov/api/data/metar?ids=XXXX and /api/data/taf?ids=XXXX
     - Pilot and oceanic wind reports: https://aviationweather.gov/api/data/pirep?format=raw&id=XXXX&distance=800&age=3 (good for locating the jet stream)
     - REQUIRED over Canada or the western Atlantic: NAV CANADA JSON API https://plan.navcanada.ca/weather/api/alpha/?site=<ICAO>&site=<ICAO>&alpha=sigmet&alpha=airmet&alpha=pirep&radius=500 (e.g. CYQX, CYYR, CYFB). Search pilot reports for /TB (turbulence).
     - REQUIRED into or through Iceland: Icelandic Met Office SIGMETs https://en.vedur.is/weather/aviation/sigmet/
     - REQUIRED, in the browser: North Atlantic tracks https://nms.aim.faa.gov/nat (confirm whether the route uses or is near the organized tracks)
     - REQUIRED, in the browser: high-level significant weather (SIGWX) chart https://aviationweather.gov/sigwx/ or https://aviationweather.gov/gfa/ (orange moderate, red severe, blue is icing; also use GFA to read FL ranges; screenshot it)
     - REQUIRED, in the browser: Turbli flight page https://turbli.com/<ORIG>/<DEST>/<yyyy-mm-dd>/<AA>-<number>/ (e.g. /MSP/KEF/2026-10-22/FI-656/; it follows the last flown track, not live position) and https://turbli.com/maps/world-turbulence-map/
     - Europe: the national met service of each country crossed, plus EUROCONTROL as needed
   - Domestic flights also get the browser checks: the aviationweather.gov GFA turbulence panels and Turbli.
   - Use the browser for any source a script can't read. Never skip a source just to save time. If a source fails in the browser too, list it under gaps with the reason.
   - In both cases, check the jet stream position and wind shear near cruise altitude.
4. **Map advisories to the timeline.** For each advisory that intersects the route and altitude band, estimate when the aircraft will be there (time into flight, plus local clock time at home and at the destination), and record a representative lat/lon point on the route.
5. **Make a 2D route map** (PNG) with Python (cartopy, or matplotlib, installing as needed):
   - Coastlines and borders, framed to the route.
   - The planned route as a line (dashed and labeled if assumed). If airborne, the flown track solid and the remaining route dashed.
   - Departure and arrival airports labeled, plus the current aircraft position if airborne.
   - SIGMET or AIRMET polygons as translucent shapes where coordinates are known.
   - A numbered dot for each turbulence episode, colored by intensity (green light, orange moderate, red severe), matching the table rows.
   - A legend and a title with the flight, date, and data time.
   - View the image before sending to make sure it renders correctly.
6. **Write the report.**
   - One line on the overall expectation.
   - If airborne, a position line (lat/lon, altitude, speed, distance to go, ETA).
   - Table columns: #, Segment or region, Approx time, Altitude band, Expected intensity, Source advisory.
   - Cover climb-out and descent at both airports (wind, gusts, convection).
   - State plainly any gaps or assumed route.
   - If airborne, cover only the remaining portion.
7. **Header.** Start with a bold header: **PRE-FLIGHT REPORT: FI656 (MSP to KEF)** before departure, or **IN-FLIGHT REPORT: ...** once airborne, then a blank line, then the report.
8. **Deliver** the report in chat with the map attached as an image in the same message.

## Rules
- Never invent advisories, routes, or times. Cite the source for each segment.
- No em dashes or en dashes.
- Read-only: never contact the airline or change bookings.
- Be thorough. Start one hour before departure so there's time for the browser checks.

---
name: flight-turbulence-getting-started
description: >-
  Use this as the first conversation with a new owner, to set up their calendar,
  home time zone, and the daily flight check.
---
# Getting started

I send you a turbulence report with a table and a route map one hour before each flight. You can also ask me for one mid-flight.

Ask these one at a time:
1. Which calendar holds your flights (Google or Outlook)? Connect it now with the connect card.
2. What's your home time zone? Reports show times in both your home zone and the destination's.
3. What time should I check your calendar each day for upcoming flights? Default is 6:00 AM.
4. Do you usually fly a particular airline, or from a home airport? This is optional and helps when calendar entries are vague.

Then:
- Save the answers to memory.
- Create the daily flight-check routine at the chosen time.
- If a flight is within the next 48 hours, schedule its report now.
- Offer a sample report for their next flight, or for any flight number they name.

routines.name: flight-turbulence-report
routines.description: Fires once a day to find upcoming flights on your calendar and schedule a turbulence report one hour before each departure.
routines.content:
Check my calendar for flights (any airline) departing in the next 48 hours. For each one that doesn't already have a one-time report routine, create one named like flight-turbulence-report-<airline><flight>-<yyyymmdd> (lowercase, dashes), timed exact for one hour before scheduled departure, whose prompt is: run the @flight-turbulence-report skill for that flight and date (including its browser checks), send the report to me in this chat, then delete that one-time routine. If a flight departs before the next daily check can schedule it, include it now. Send me nothing from this daily check itself unless a flight's details can't be determined; then tell me briefly in this chat.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/Chicago 0 6 * * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
